passage:
I'm Chinmay, and in my first month at the hostel in Manipal I said yes to everything. Instant noodles on the terrace at midnight, yes. A trip to the beach at six in the morning, yes. A quiz club I had no interest in, also yes. My room felt too quiet otherwise.
Thomas was in the room opposite, from Kottayam. On the fourth night we both admitted we'd cried after our parents left. By the second week we were sharing a toothpaste tube and finishing each other's jokes, and I told Amma on the phone that I'd found my best friend.
Looking back, I'm a little embarrassed by how fast I said that. We'd known each other eleven days. The warmth was real, but a lot of it was two homesick boys holding on to the first person who understood. We're still friends. Just the ordinary, slower kind.

qa.q: What did Thomas and Chinmay admit on the fourth night?
qa.a: They both admitted they'd cried after their parents left.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay say yes to every invitation in the first month?
qa.a: Chinmay was lonely and the room felt too quiet otherwise, so every plan was a way not to be alone.

qa.q: What could Chinmay keep in mind during this open-door stage?
qa.a: Chinmay could enjoy the quick warmth while letting friendships grow at their own pace, instead of naming someone a best friend after eleven days.

qa.q: How might Thomas have felt in those first weeks?
qa.a: Thomas was homesick too, so finding Chinmay across the corridor probably felt like relief and a safe person to hold on to.

grounding: Shows a lonely, eager first-year hostel student saying yes to everything and forming a quick, homesick closeness that felt stronger than it yet was.

passage:
Trainee batch note, week three. From the training coordinator.
Saurabh (from Patna, first job, first time living away from home) has joined every plan in the batch so far: the Friday biryani run, the Sunday fort trek, even the badminton group, though he told me he "can't really play". He is always the first to reply "I'm in" on the batch group.
He and Sonali, from Guwahati, seem to have become very close very quickly. I often see them in the cafeteria after nine, talking about home food and their mothers' phone calls. Last week Sonali said to me, laughing, "He's already like my brother."
It is lovely to see, and it is helping both of them settle. I have also noticed that Saurabh looks lost on evenings when no plan is on. I've paired him with a senior buddy for the next month and will mention the wellness sessions at our check-in.

qa.q: What does Saurabh reply on the batch group?
qa.a: Saurabh is always the first to reply 'I'm in' on the batch group.

qa.q: Why might Saurabh join every plan, even badminton?
qa.a: Saurabh is far from home for the first time and probably lonely; saying yes keeps away the empty evenings, which is when he looks lost.

qa.q: What did the coordinator do well to support Saurabh at this stage?
qa.a: The coordinator noticed the pattern without judging it, paired Saurabh with a senior buddy and planned to mention the wellness sessions, giving steadier support than one fast friendship.

qa.q: How might Sonali see the closeness with Saurabh?
qa.a: Sonali seems to enjoy it and already calls him like a brother, because sharing homesickness makes the bond feel strong very fast.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult in a first-job city saying yes to every invitation, with shared homesickness creating quick closeness.
